conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here—adjusting to life with a new baby can be joyful, overwhelming, and everything in between.  

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to do a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s a 10-question check-in that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping during the first postpartum year. Anything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you.  

We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to start?

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[sighs softly, eyes a little tired]  
Not as much as I used to. I mean, I still laugh when my husband makes a goofy face at the baby, but it feels kind of muted—like I have to remind myself to smile. Most of the time I’m just… tired and distracted worrying about whether she’s eating enough or breathing okay in her sleep.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I guess I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. Sometimes I’ll chuckle if the baby makes a silly face, yet it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug, eyes on the floor for a second]  
Not really. I mean, I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it feels like I’m just getting through the day. I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like myself again,” but when tomorrow comes, it’s the same fog. Everything feels more like an obligation than something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday—she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking maybe I’d overstimulated her or missed her sleepy window. Logically I know babies just have rough days, but I still caught myself thinking, “If I were better at reading her cues she wouldn’t be crying.” It’s not constant, but little things like that pop into my head a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be holding her while she’s napping and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking something might be wrong even though she’s breathing fine. Or I’ll lie in bed at night running through all the “what-ifs”—what if she chokes, what if I fall asleep and don’t hear her, what if I’m doing everything wrong? There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits there like background noise.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week. Nothing full-blown, but I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I need to check the baby cam right away or something bad’s about to happen. It passes in a few minutes, but it leaves me kind of shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the minute I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to get her down—there’s another thing waiting. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles and the laundry pile and just think, “I can’t keep up.” I’m managing, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and running on empty.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy,” more… keyed-up. Once she finally goes down around 10, I lie there replaying every little sound she made, wondering if she’ll wake up early or if I’ll hear her over the monitor. Takes me an hour or two to drift off, and then I’m up every couple of hours to check on her. So it’s not that I’m crying myself to sleep—just can’t shut my brain off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. It’s not all day, but it hits in waves—like yesterday afternoon, everything was technically fine, yet I just felt heavy and wanted to curl up under a blanket. It usually passes if I keep busy, but the low mood keeps sneaking back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No… I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of evenings, like the sadness is right behind my eyes, but it never tips over into real tears. Mostly I just feel kind of numb and tired instead.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I could never leave my baby like that.

You've shared how the early weeks with your baby have felt heavy and foggy: laughter comes out forced, activities you once enjoyed now feel like chores, and waves of sadness catch you off-guard. You described daily <sym>anxiety</sym> with chest tightness, racing-heart moments, and nights spent replaying every baby sound instead of sleeping. While you love your daughter and know you would never harm yourself, you're running on empty and wondering if you'll ever feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter now feels forced and diminished, aligning with 'definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Her description of persistent anhedonia and feeling only obligation aligns with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times a week" for minor mishaps, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, excessive worries about infant safety with no real trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys frequent difficulty coping ('I can't keep up', 'running on empty') but still managing, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep linked to anxious rumination about the baby, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms feeling sad "some of the time" with recurring waves of heaviness, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score 19 (cut-off 14) indicates probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. She endorses core symptoms: persistent sad/flat mood (<quote>same fog</quote>), marked loss of interest (<quote>everything feels more like an obligation</quote>), daily self-blame, and functional impairment (<quote>running on empty</quote>). Associated <sym>anxiety</sym> symptoms meet criteria for comorbid <med>generalized anxiety disorder</med> (near-constant worry, muscle tension, sleep disturbance). No suicidal ideation (Q10=0), protective factor voiced (<quote>I could never leave my baby</quote>). Score pattern aligns with DSM-5 threshold for further evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within 1 week
2. Discuss <med>psychotherapy</med> options (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> if moderate-severe
3. Provide education on postpartum depression/anxiety; normalize that recovery is common with support
4. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walk and acceptance of household tasks left undone
5. Promote sleep hygiene: 4-hour maximum wake window, tag-team night duties with partner when possible
6. Offer local support group contacts and 24/7 warmline numbers for crisis support
7. Arrange EPDS re-screen at 2 weeks to track progress after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Screening note – Postpartum mood/anxiety screen  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy,” episodic sadness most days  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal enjoyment, activities feel obligatory  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, chest tightness, “what-if” rumination  
- Two panic-tinged episodes this week (sudden racing heart, urge to check baby)  
- Self-blaming cognitions re infant care several times/week  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties linked to hyper-arousal, not low mood per se  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “running on empty,” unable to keep up with tasks  
- No tearful episodes; describes numbness rather than overt crying  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (strong protective factor: “I could never leave my baby”)

Pattern  
Consistent with sub-threshold to moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; functional impact evident in sleep, coping, and daily task management. No safety concerns identified at present.

Risk flags  
✓ Low mood, anhedonia, guilt cognitions  
✓ Anxiety/panic symptoms  
✓ Sleep disruption secondary to mental arousal  
✗ No suicidal or infanticidal thoughts reported

Plan  
Continue monitoring; consider standardized EPDS and differential screening for GAD; provide psycho-education, support resources, and expedited outpatient follow-up within 1–2 weeks.
